title: Greetings
description: Hello and goodbye across the day, with formality notes.

steps.title: A soft start
steps.body: Japanese greetings shift with time of day and how well you know someone. Learn a small set well rather than many poorly.

steps.title: Form vs. familiarity
steps.body: Use polite forms with strangers, older people, and formal situations. Casual forms are for friends, family, and peers.
bullets: おはようございます is the standard morning greeting.
こんにちは works from late morning through afternoon.
こんばんは is used in the evening.
じゃあね / またね are friendly and informal — both hi/bye vibes.

items.note: When someone is going to sleep

items.meaning: Take care / see you later (to someone leaving)

phrases.target: こんにちは、お元気ですか？
元気です、ありがとう。あなたは？

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese greeting with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, how are you?":
steps.targetSentence: こんにちは、お元気ですか？
steps.explanation: A warm, time-appropriate greeting — the foundation of any first impression.

steps.title: Listen · evening
steps.prompt: You hear this in the evening. What does it mean?
steps.explanation: こんばんは is the standard evening greeting.

steps.partnerSays: こんにちは、はじめまして。お元気ですか？
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Hello, nice to meet you. How are you?
steps.prompt: Reply politely:
options: はい、元気です。ありがとうございます。
steps.correctAnswer: はい、元気です。ありがとうございます。
steps.explanation: "はい、元気です。ありがとうございます" answers warmly in polite form. "さようなら" is a goodbye.

steps.title: Check · time of day
steps.prompt: Which greeting fits the evening?
steps.explanation: こんばんは is the natural evening greeting.

steps.title: Check · formality
steps.prompt: You meet your friend’s parent for the first time. Best choice?
options: こんにちは、お元気ですか？
steps.explanation: Polite こんにちは + お元気ですか keeps things respectful with someone new and older.

steps.title: Check · going to sleep
steps.prompt: You’re heading to bed and want to say good night. You say…
steps.explanation: おやすみなさい is reserved for when someone is actually going to sleep.

title: Please & thank you
description: Politeness formulas that open every exchange.

steps.title: Small words, big difference
steps.body: Japanese service and street interactions expect ください and ありがとう. Skipping them can sound abrupt even when you don’t mean it.

steps.title: Politeness levels
steps.body: ください is the everyday “please.” お願いします is a bit more formal/request-like.
bullets: ありがとうございます = thank you (polite).
どうも = casual thanks / hi.
すみません can mean excuse me or sorry, depending on tone.
ごめんなさい is a clearer apology than すみません.

items.term: ありがとうございます

phrases.target: ありがとうございます。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese polite phrase with its English meaning:

pairs.foreign: ありがとうございます

steps.prompt: Arrange the stones to say: "A coffee, please.":
steps.targetSentence: コーヒーをください。
steps.explanation: Combining a request with "please" — the cornerstone of polite interaction.

steps.title: Listen · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says ありがとう. A polite reply is…

steps.partnerSays: はい、どうぞ。三百円です。
steps.prompt: Thank her as you pay:
options: ありがとうございます。
steps.correctAnswer: ありがとうございます。
steps.explanation: "ありがとうございます" is the polite thank-you. "どういたしまして" is what the clerk would say back to you.

steps.title: Check · shop
steps.prompt: How do you say “please” when asking for something in a shop?
steps.explanation: 〜をください is the standard way to request an item.

steps.title: Check · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says ありがとう. A polite reply is…
steps.explanation: どういたしまして is the standard “you’re welcome.”

title: Numbers 1–10
description: Count clearly for prices, times, and quantities.

steps.title: Count slowly
steps.body: Japanese numbers are used constantly — prices, platform numbers, ages. Rhythm first; speed later.

steps.title: Counters & reading
steps.body: Native Japanese numbers (ひとつ, ふたつ…) are common for small quantities of objects. Sino-Japanese (いち, に…) dominate for time, money, and larger numbers.
bullets: いち, に, さん… for most counting.
ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ… for “how many things.”
Learn numbers in short phrases, not only as a list.

phrases.target: コーヒーを二つください。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese number with its numeral:
Arrange the stones to say: "Two coffees, please.":
steps.targetSentence: コーヒーを二つください。
steps.explanation: Numbers in context — the essential combination for real-world transactions.

steps.title: Listen · age
steps.prompt: Someone says this. How old are they?
steps.explanation: 二十歳 (はたち) = twenty years old.

steps.partnerSays: チケットは何枚ですか？
steps.prompt: Ask for two tickets:
steps.correctAnswer: 二枚お願いします。
steps.explanation: "二枚お願いします" uses the counter 枚 for flat objects like tickets. "千五百円です" is the price the clerk would quote.

steps.title: Check · seven
steps.prompt: What is “seven” in Japanese?
steps.explanation: なな (or しち) is seven.

steps.title: Check · phrase
steps.prompt: “コーヒーを二つ” means…
steps.explanation: 二つ means two (left counter).

steps.title: Check · age
steps.prompt: How do you say “I am twenty years old”?
steps.explanation: Age uses 〜歳: 二十歳です.

title: Introduce yourself
description: Name, origin, and a simple nice-to-meet-you.

steps.title: First contact
steps.body: A short self-introduction is enough: name, where you’re from, and a polite close.

items.term: よろしくお願いします
items.meaning: Please treat me well / Looking forward to working with you

steps.title: はじめまして & よろしくお願いします
steps.body: At a first meeting, はじめまして is almost always followed by よろしくお願いします. It softens the introduction and shows goodwill.

phrases.target: こんにちは、アレックスです。
はじめまして。よろしくお願いします。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese introduction phrase with its English meaning:

pairs.foreign: よろしくお願いします

steps.prompt: Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, my name is Alex.":
steps.targetSentence: こんにちは、アレックスです。
steps.explanation: Your origin in one clear sentence — the natural follow-up to sharing your name.

steps.title: Listen · origin
steps.prompt: What does this person say?

steps.partnerSays: はじめまして。レアです。どこから来ましたか？
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Hajimemashite. Rea desu. Doko kara kimashita ka?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Nice to meet you. I'm Lea. Where are you from?
steps.prompt: Say where you're from and return the question:
options: アメリカから来ました。レアさんは？
steps.correctAnswer: アメリカから来ました。レアさんは？
steps.explanation: "アメリカから来ました。レアさんは？" answers her question and returns it using her name + さん, which is more natural than あなた.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “サムです” means…
steps.explanation: 〜です after a name = my name is…

steps.title: Check · origin
steps.prompt: Best line for “I come from Belgium”?
options: ベルギーに住んでいます
ベルギーから来ました
steps.explanation: 〜から来ました expresses origin.

title: Colors & simple descriptions
description: Name colors and describe everyday objects.

steps.title: Painting with words
steps.body: Colors in Japanese are often nouns or な-adjectives. Many take の when modifying a noun (赤い車 → 赤の車 is also heard, but the い-adjective form is standard).

steps.title: Color forms
steps.body: Most basic colors are い-adjectives (赤い, 青い…). A few are nouns (ピンク, オレンジ) and need の.
bullets: 赤い車 = a red car
青い空 = blue sky
ピンクの服 = pink clothes

phrases.target: 彼女は緑のバッグを持っています。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese color with its English name:
Arrange the stones to say: "a blue dress":
steps.targetSentence: 青いドレス
steps.explanation: Color + polite form — everything needed to express a preference in any shop.

steps.title: Listen · color
steps.prompt: You hear “青いドレス”. What is being described?

steps.partnerSays: どの色がいいですか？
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Dono iro ga ii desu ka?
steps.prompt: Say you want the red one:
steps.correctAnswer: 赤いのが欲しいです。
steps.explanation: "赤いのが欲しいです" (I want the red one) answers the question about color directly.

steps.title: Check · color
steps.prompt: How do you say “a blue dress”?
steps.explanation: 青い is the い-adjective form that directly modifies the noun.

steps.title: Check · noun color
steps.prompt: Which color is typically used with の?
steps.explanation: Loanword colors like ピンク and オレンジ usually take の: ピンクの服.

title: At the café
description: Order drinks and ask for the bill with confidence.

steps.title: A quiet table
steps.body: 〜をください plus a smile covers most orders. Add numbers and sizes when you need them.

steps.title: Café vocabulary culture
steps.body: コーヒー often means a regular coffee. アイスコーヒー is iced; ホット is hot.
bullets: 店内 = for here
持ち帰り = to go
お会計 = the bill
Tipping is not expected in Japan.

phrases.source: I would like a coffee, please.

phrases.target: お茶を持ち帰りでください。
お会計をお願いします。
店内ですか、持ち帰りですか？

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese café word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I would like a coffee, please.":
steps.targetSentence: コーヒーをください。
steps.targetTranslation: I would like a coffee, please.
steps.explanation: A polite order that works in any café — commit it to memory for the first sip.

steps.title: Listen · bill
steps.prompt: What is being asked for?
steps.audioText: お会計をお願いします

steps.partnerSays: 店内ですか、お持ち帰りですか？
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Tennai desu ka, omochikaeri desu ka?

steps.prompt: You're staying at the café. Answer:
options: お会計をお願いします。
アイスコーヒーをください。
steps.correctAnswer: 店内でお願いします。
steps.explanation: "店内でお願いします" means you'll have it here. "お会計をお願いします" is for asking for the bill later.

steps.title: Check · bill
steps.prompt: How do you ask for the bill?
options: お会計をお願いします。
steps.explanation: お会計 is the standard word for the bill in a café or restaurant.

steps.title: Check · to go
steps.prompt: “持ち帰り” means…
steps.explanation: 持ち帰り = takeaway / to go.

title: At the market
description: Fruit, quantities, and polite requests at a stall.

steps.title: Market pace
steps.body: Markets reward clear numbers and 〜をください. Pointing plus a word still works — language makes it smoother.

phrases.target: りんごを三つください。
トマトを一キロください。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese market word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I’d like three apples, please.":
steps.targetSentence: りんごを三つください。
steps.explanation: Quantity, item, price question — the complete phrase for any market stall.

steps.title: Listen · price
steps.prompt: What is the stallholder asking?

steps.partnerSays: 他に何か？
steps.prompt: Ask for three apples and the price:
options: りんごも三つ。いくらですか？
今日はいい天気ですね。
steps.correctAnswer: りんごも三つ。いくらですか？
steps.explanation: "りんごも三つ。いくらですか？" adds to your order and asks the total. "五百円です" is what the seller would say.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “いくらですか？” asks for…
steps.explanation: いくら means “how much,” so いくらですか asks about price.

steps.title: Check · order
steps.prompt: Best for “three apples, please”?
options: りんごを三つください
コーヒーを三つください
さようなら りんご
steps.explanation: りんごを三つください directly matches the request.

title: Small talk & weather
description: Light conversation beyond hello.

steps.title: Beyond こんにちは
steps.body: Weather and weekend questions are safe bridges after greetings.

phrases.target: 今日はいい天気ですね。
雨がたくさん降っています。
外は凍えるように寒いです！

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese weather phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Nice weather today.":
steps.targetSentence: 今日はいい天気ですね。
steps.explanation: A light observation that opens the door to warm, easy conversation.

steps.title: Listen · rain
steps.prompt: What does this mean?
steps.audioText: 雨がたくさん降っています

steps.partnerSays: 今日はいい天気ですね！
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Kyō wa ii tenki desu ne!
steps.prompt: Agree and keep the chat going:
options: はい、晴れですね。週末はどうでしたか？
いいえ、コーヒーは好きじゃないです。
お会計をお願いします。
steps.correctAnswer: はい、晴れですね。週末はどうでしたか？
steps.explanation: Agreeing with ね and asking about the weekend is classic small talk that keeps the exchange flowing.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “雨が降っています” means…
steps.explanation: 雨が降る = to rain.

steps.title: Check · weekend
steps.prompt: How do you ask “How was your weekend?” politely?
steps.explanation: どうでしたか asks about a past event politely.

title: At the restaurant
description: Reservations, ordering a meal, and dietary needs.

steps.title: From table to bill
steps.body: A Japanese meal follows a calm rhythm: greeting, being seated, ordering, and eventually asking for the bill — nobody rushes you.

steps.title: Menu know-how
steps.body: メニュー is the list of dishes. 定食 is a set meal.
bullets: 前菜 / サラダ is often the starter.
メイン / 主菜 is the main course.
Say いただきます before eating and ごちそうさまでした after.

phrases.target: 二人用のテーブルをお願いします。
ピーナッツアレルギーがあります。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese restaurant word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "A table for two, please.":
steps.targetSentence: 二人用のテーブルをお願いします。
steps.explanation: The natural, confident way to place an order with any server.

steps.title: Listen · recommendation
steps.prompt: What is being asked?

steps.partnerSays: ご注文はお決まりですか？
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Have you decided on your order?
steps.prompt: Order the fish:
options: 次の停留所で降ります。
steps.correctAnswer: 魚にします。
steps.explanation: "〜にします" is the standard way to state your choice when ordering.

steps.title: Check · set meal
steps.prompt: In a Japanese restaurant, “定食” usually refers to…
options: The full list of every dish
steps.explanation: 定食 is a set meal; the full list is メニュー.

steps.title: Check · vegetarian
steps.prompt: How do you say “I’m vegetarian”?
options: ベジタリアンがあります
ベジタリアンをください
ベジタリアンにします
steps.explanation: 〜です states what you are.

title: Talking about plans
description: Use 〜つもり / 〜予定 and the volitional to talk about near-future plans.

steps.title: The near future
steps.body: Japanese often uses 〜つもりです (intend to) or plain dictionary form + 予定 to talk about plans.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Subject + verb stem/dictionary form + つもりです / 予定です.
bullets: 食べるつもりです = I intend to eat
行く予定です = I plan to go
映画を見ます = I’ll watch a movie (simple non-past)

items.meaning: I plan to… / It is scheduled…

phrases.source: What are you going to do this weekend?
phrases.target: 今週末は何をするつもりですか？

phrases.source: I’m going to visit my parents.
phrases.target: 両親に会うつもりです。

phrases.source: We’re going to watch a film.
She’s going to travel to Kyoto.
phrases.target: 彼女は京都に旅行する予定です。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese plan or intention form with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I’m going to visit my parents.":
steps.targetSentence: 両親に会うつもりです。
steps.targetTranslation: I’m going to visit my parents.
steps.explanation: Future marker + plan — two building blocks for any upcoming arrangement.

steps.title: Listen · structure
steps.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses intention?

steps.partnerSays: 今週末は何をするつもり？
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Konshūmatsu wa nani o suru tsumori?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: What are you planning to do this weekend?
steps.prompt: Say you're planning to see your parents:
options: 両親に会うつもりです。
steps.correctAnswer: 両親に会うつもりです。
steps.explanation: "両親に会うつもりです" uses 〜つもり to express a plan or intention.

steps.title: Check · structure
steps.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses “intend to”?
steps.explanation: Dictionary form + つもりです.

steps.title: Check · translate
steps.prompt: “映画を見る予定です” means…
options: We are going to watch a film
We want to watch a film
steps.explanation: 〜予定です describes a plan.

title: Simple directions
description: left, right, straight — and asking where something is.

steps.title: Finding your way
steps.body: Combine どこですか with a few direction words for short walks in a new city.

phrases.target: まっすぐ行って、それから左です。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese direction word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Go straight ahead, then left.":
steps.targetSentence: まっすぐ行って、それから左です。
steps.explanation: Left, right, and straight — three words that will get you anywhere in the city.

steps.title: Listen · where
steps.prompt: What is being asked?

steps.partnerSays: まっすぐ行って、それから左です。薬局の向かいです。
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Massugu itte, sorekara hidari desu. Yakkyoku no mukai desu.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Go straight, then left. It's across from the pharmacy.
steps.prompt: Ask whether it's far:
steps.correctAnswer: 遠いですか？
steps.explanation: "遠いですか？" is the natural follow-up after getting directions.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “まっすぐ” means…
steps.explanation: まっすぐ means straight ahead.

steps.title: Check · ask
steps.prompt: “駅はどこですか？” asks for…
steps.explanation: どこですか = where is…

title: Travel phrases
description: Tickets, platforms, and delays.

steps.title: On the move
steps.body: Stations and airports repeat the same patterns: destination, platform, delay, seat.

phrases.target: 京都までの切符をください。
東京までの往復をお願いします。

どこで乗り換えますか？

steps.targetSentence: 京都までの切符をください。

steps.title: Listen · delay

steps.partnerSays: 三番線から出ます。
steps.prompt: Ask if the train is running late:
options: 電車は遅れていますか？
京都までの切符をください。
今日はいい天気ですね。
steps.correctAnswer: 電車は遅れていますか？
steps.explanation: "電車は遅れていますか？" asks about delays using the ています form for a current state.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “切符” means…
steps.explanation: 切符 is a ticket.

steps.title: Check · delay
steps.prompt: “遅れています” means…
steps.explanation: 遅れ = delay; 遅れています = is delayed.

title: At the hotel
description: Check-in lines and simple room requests.

steps.title: Front desk
steps.body: Reservation, nights, and room type cover most check-ins.

phrases.target: 朝食は含まれていますか？
チェックアウトは何時ですか？

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese hotel word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have a reservation.":
steps.targetSentence: 予約しています。
steps.explanation: A short statement that confirms your booking and sets check-in in motion.

steps.title: Listen · breakfast
steps.prompt: What is being asked?
steps.audioText: 朝食は含まれていますか
options: Do you have a double room?

steps.partnerSays: いらっしゃいませ。二泊ですね？
steps.prompt: Confirm and ask about breakfast:
options: はい。朝食は含まれていますか？
いいえ、コーヒーは好きじゃないです。
りんごを三つください。
steps.correctAnswer: はい。朝食は含まれていますか？
steps.explanation: "はい。朝食は含まれていますか？" confirms the booking and asks a useful check-in question.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “予約しています” means…
steps.explanation: 予約しています = I have a reservation.

steps.title: Check · checkout
steps.prompt: How do you ask what time checkout is?
options: チェックアウトは何時ですか？
フロントはどこですか？
steps.explanation: チェックアウトは何時ですか is the standard question.

title: Getting around town
description: Buses, metro, taxis, and buying tickets.

steps.title: Moving through the city
steps.body: Most cities run on a mix of metro, bus, and train — one word (切符, 定期券) covers most fare questions.

phrases.target: 一番近い地下鉄の駅はどこですか？

phrases.source: Does this bus go to the center?
phrases.target: このバスは市内中心部に行きますか？

phrases.source: I’m getting off at the next stop.
phrases.target: 次の停留所で降ります。

phrases.source: Can you call me a taxi?
phrases.target: タクシーを呼んでくれますか？

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese transport word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Where’s the nearest metro station?":
steps.targetSentence: 一番近い地下鉄の駅はどこですか？
steps.explanation: The phrase that ends any bus or metro journey gracefully.

steps.title: Listen · getting off
steps.prompt: What does this mean?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Yes, it goes to the city center.
steps.prompt: Say you're getting off at the next stop:
options: 次の停留所で降ります。
京都までの切符をください。
両親に会うつもりです。
steps.correctAnswer: 次の停留所で降ります。
steps.explanation: "次の停留所で降ります" tells the driver where you want to get off.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “定期券” usually refers to…
options: A day or week / month pass
steps.explanation: 定期券 is a commuter / period pass.

steps.title: Check · getting off
steps.prompt: How do you say “I’m getting off here”?
steps.explanation: 降りる = to get off.

title: Pharmacy & feeling unwell
description: Describe symptoms and get help at a pharmacy or doctor’s.

steps.title: Green cross, calm help
steps.body: Japanese pharmacies (薬局) can advise on minor issues before you need a doctor.

steps.title: 〜が痛い
steps.body: The most useful pattern for pain is body part + が痛い.
bullets: 頭が痛い = I have a headache
お腹が痛い = I have a stomach ache
歯が痛い = my teeth hurt

phrases.source: Do you have something for a sore throat?

phrases.target: 救急車を呼んでください！

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese health phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have a headache.":
steps.targetSentence: 頭が痛いです。
steps.explanation: Describing the most common ache — clear and calm gets you the right remedy.

steps.title: Listen · stomach
steps.prompt: Which phrase means “I have a stomach ache”?

steps.partnerSays: 処方箋はありますか？
steps.prompt: Say no and ask for throat medicine:
options: いいえ。喉の薬はありますか？
steps.correctAnswer: いいえ。喉の薬はありますか？
steps.explanation: "いいえ。喉の薬はありますか？" answers the question and asks for an over-the-counter remedy.

steps.title: Check · pattern
steps.prompt: How do you say “I have a stomach ache”?
steps.explanation: Body part + が痛い.

steps.title: Check · emergency
steps.prompt: Which phrase calls for urgent help?
steps.explanation: 助けて！ is the standard cry for help.

title: Telling time
description: Ask for and give the time, on the hour and beyond.

steps.title: 今何時ですか？
steps.body: Japanese uses the 24-hour clock for schedules, but everyday speech uses 時 and 分 with 午前 / 午後 when needed.

steps.title: Minute expressions
steps.body: Learn these fixed chunks.
bullets: 〜時 = o’clock
半 = half past
〜分 = minutes
正午 / 夜中 = noon / midnight

phrases.target: 電車は十四時三十分に出ます。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese time expression with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "It’s half past seven.":
steps.targetSentence: 七時半です。
steps.explanation: Hour + "half" — the most common time expression in everyday conversation.

steps.title: Listen · half past
steps.prompt: What time is being said?

steps.partnerSays: 十四時三十分です。
steps.prompt: Thank her and say when your train leaves:
options: ありがとうございます。電車は十五時に出ます。
すみません、今何時ですか？
steps.correctAnswer: ありがとうございます。電車は十五時に出ます。
steps.explanation: "ありがとうございます。電車は十五時に出ます" thanks her and uses the 24-hour clock, common on Japanese timetables.

steps.title: Check · half past
steps.prompt: How do you say “half past seven”?
steps.explanation: 半 after the hour = half past.

steps.title: Check · noon
steps.prompt: “正午です” means…
steps.explanation: 正午 is noon; 夜中 / 真夜中 is midnight.

title: Days, months & dates
description: The calendar in Japanese, and how to say a date.

steps.title: The week starts on Monday
steps.body: Japanese calendars typically start the week with 月曜日 (Monday).

steps.title: Saying a date
steps.body: Japanese dates go year → month → day. For the day, special readings exist for 1–10 and a few others.
bullets: 五月一日 = May 1st (ごがつついたち)
五月二日 = May 2nd (ふつか)
Days of the week are not capitalized.

phrases.target: 誕生日は五月一日です。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese day with its English name:
Arrange the stones to say: "My birthday is May 1st.":
steps.targetSentence: 誕生日は五月一日です。
steps.explanation: A date in full — once you know the pattern, every date falls into place.

steps.title: Listen · day
steps.prompt: What day is mentioned?

steps.partnerSays: 今日は何曜日？
steps.prompt: Say it's Wednesday:
steps.correctAnswer: 水曜日です。
steps.explanation: "水曜日です" answers with the day of the week. 曜日 is the ending for all weekday names.

steps.title: Check · order
steps.prompt: Which day comes right after 水曜日?
steps.explanation: 月火水木金土日.

steps.title: Check · capitalization
steps.prompt: In Japanese, days and months are…
options: Written with kanji or kana, no English-style capitals
steps.explanation: Japanese does not use Latin capitals; days/months use kanji.

title: Talking about family
description: Name family members and describe relationships.

steps.title: Who’s who
steps.body: Family vocabulary combines with います / います and possessives like 私の.

steps.title: My vs. your family
steps.body: Japanese often uses humble words for one’s own family and respectful words for others’.
bullets: 父 / お父さん = my father / someone else’s father
母 / お母さん = my mother / someone else’s mother
兄弟 = siblings

phrases.target: 両親は東京に住んでいます。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese family word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have two brothers.":
steps.targetSentence: 兄弟が二人います。
steps.explanation: A warm, simple statement that naturally invites the other person to share too.

steps.title: Listen · sister
steps.prompt: What does “私の姉” mean?

steps.partnerSays: はじめまして。兄弟はいますか？
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Nice to meet you. Do you have siblings?
steps.prompt: Say you have two younger brothers:
options: いいえ、お腹は空いていません。
steps.correctAnswer: はい、弟が二人います。
steps.explanation: "はい、弟が二人います" answers directly, using います for people and the counter 人.

steps.title: Check · possessive
steps.prompt: How do you say “my sister” (older)?
steps.explanation: 姉 = older sister.

steps.title: Check · plural
steps.prompt: “両親” means…
steps.explanation: 両親 = both parents.

title: Shopping for clothes
description: Sizes, trying things on, and asking about price.

steps.title: Trying it on
steps.body: Clothes shopping mixes size, color, and a few polite requests to try things on or ask for a different size.

items.term: ドレス / ワンピース
大きすぎる / 小さすぎる

phrases.source: Do you have this in a size M?

phrases.target: 試着してもいいですか？

phrases.source: Do you have a bigger size?
phrases.target: もっと大きいサイズはありますか？

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese shopping word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Do you have this in a size M?":
steps.targetSentence: Mサイズはありますか？
steps.targetTranslation: Do you have this in a size M?
steps.explanation: The one question that keeps a shopping trip moving in the right direction.

steps.title: Listen · size
steps.prompt: What does this mean?

steps.partnerSays: はい、試着室はあちらです。
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Yes, the fitting room is over there.
steps.prompt: After trying it on, say it's too small and ask for a bigger size:
options: 小さすぎます。もっと大きいサイズはありますか？
試着してもいいですか？
steps.correctAnswer: 小さすぎます。もっと大きいサイズはありますか？
steps.explanation: "小さすぎます。もっと大きいサイズはありますか？" describes the problem with 〜すぎます and asks for the next size up.

steps.title: Check · size
steps.prompt: How do you ask “do you have this in a size M?”
steps.explanation: 〜サイズはありますか is the standard size question.

steps.title: Check · too small
steps.prompt: “小さすぎます” means…
steps.explanation: 小さすぎる = too small.

title: Particles & basic structure
description: は, が, を, に — the glue of Japanese sentences.

steps.title: Particles mark roles
steps.body: Japanese uses particles instead of word order or articles to show the role of each noun.

steps.title: Core particles
steps.body: Memorize new nouns with a typical particle.
bullets: は = topic marker
が = subject marker (often new info)
を = direct object
に / へ = direction / time / indirect object
で = location of action / means

steps.title: Check · topic
steps.prompt: Which particle marks the topic?
steps.explanation: は is the topic marker.

steps.title: Check · object
steps.prompt: Which particle marks the direct object?
steps.explanation: を marks the thing being acted on.

steps.title: Check · location of action
steps.prompt: “図書館で勉強します” — which particle shows where the action happens?
steps.explanation: で marks the location where an action takes place.

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese particle with its function:
Arrange the stones to say: "I drink coffee.":
steps.targetSentence: 私はコーヒーを飲みます。
steps.explanation: A compact phrase that puts the article or gender rule into immediate practice.

steps.title: Listen · particle
steps.prompt: Which particle is used for the object in “本を読みます”?

steps.partnerSays: 「本を読みます」の「を」は何ですか？
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: "Hon o yomimasu" no "o" wa nan desu ka?
steps.prompt: Explain the particle:
options: 目的語のマーカーです。
steps.correctAnswer: 目的語のマーカーです。
steps.explanation: を marks the direct object of the verb. が/は mark the subject or topic, and で/に mark location.

title: です & います / あります
description: The two building blocks you’ll use every day.

steps.title: Workhorses
steps.body: です links nouns/adjectives to a topic. います (animate) and あります (inanimate) express existence.

items.term: 〜ではありません / 〜じゃないです

phrases.source: There is a book on the table.
phrases.target: テーブルの上に本があります。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese copula or existence form with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I am tired.":
steps.targetSentence: 疲れています。
steps.explanation: Two core verbs in a single sentence — a powerful combination to internalize.

steps.title: Listen · existence
steps.prompt: What does “本があります” mean?

steps.partnerSays: 元気ですか？
steps.prompt: Say you're a bit tired and hungry:
options: 少し疲れています。お腹が空いています。
steps.correctAnswer: 少し疲れています。お腹が空いています。
steps.explanation: States like being tired or hungry use the ています form: 疲れています, お腹が空いています. A plain verb + です is ungrammatical.

steps.title: Check · です
steps.prompt: “日本人です” means…
steps.explanation: 〜です after a noun = is / am.

steps.title: Check · existence
steps.prompt: “予約があります” uses…
steps.explanation: あります for inanimate things (a reservation).

steps.title: Check · animate
steps.prompt: “猫がいます” means…
steps.explanation: います is used for living things.

title: ます-form verbs
description: The polite present/future form of Japanese verbs.

steps.title: The polite form
steps.body: Most beginner Japanese starts with the ます-form. It works for present and near-future and is polite by default.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body: Dictionary form → remove う-ending sound and add ます (group rules vary).
bullets: 食べます = eat / will eat
行きます = go / will go
見ます = see / watch / will see

phrases.target: 日本語を少し話します。
彼らは日本料理が好きです。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese ます-form verb with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I speak a little Japanese.":
steps.targetSentence: 日本語を少し話します。
steps.explanation: The verb pattern in action — master this form and unlock a whole verb family.

steps.title: Listen · verb
steps.prompt: What does “食べます” mean?

steps.partnerSays: 日本語を話しますか？
steps.prompt: Say yes, you speak a little:
steps.correctAnswer: はい、少し話します。
steps.explanation: The polite form of 話す is 話します: change the final -u to -i and add ます.

steps.title: Check · form
steps.prompt: What is the polite form of “eat”?
steps.explanation: ます-form is the polite non-past.

steps.title: Check · meaning
steps.prompt: “八時に食べます” means…
options: I eat / will eat at eight
I want to eat at eight
steps.explanation: ます-form covers present and future.

title: い- and な-adjectives
description: Describe things with the two main adjective types.

steps.title: Two families of adjectives
steps.body: Japanese adjectives split into い-adjectives and な-adjectives. Both can end a sentence with です or modify a noun.

steps.title: The basic rules
steps.body: い-adjectives drop い and add くない for negative; な-adjectives use じゃない / ではありません.
bullets: 高い → 高くない
静か（な） → 静かじゃない
Both take です in polite speech when predicative.

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese adjective with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "She is small.":
steps.targetSentence: 彼女は小さいです。
steps.explanation: Agreement at work: the adjective shifts to match the noun it describes.

steps.title: Listen · type
steps.prompt: Which is a な-adjective?

steps.partnerSays: 彼は背が高いですね。彼女は？
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Kare wa se ga takai desu ne. Kanojo wa?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: He's tall, isn't he? What about her?
steps.prompt: Say she's tall too:
options: 彼女も背が高いなです。
彼女も背が高いだです。
steps.correctAnswer: 彼女も背が高いです。
steps.explanation: い-adjectives like 高い connect directly to です with no extra な or だ. Japanese adjectives don't change for gender.

steps.title: Check · い-adjective
steps.prompt: How do you say “she is small”?
steps.explanation: い-adjective + です for polite predication.

steps.title: Check · な-adjective
steps.prompt: Which adjective needs な before a noun?
steps.explanation: な-adjectives take な when modifying a noun: 静かな町.

title: Saying no
description: Turn any sentence negative with the basic Japanese negation patterns.

steps.title: Negative forms
steps.body: ます-form becomes ません. です becomes ではありません / じゃないです. い-adjectives become 〜くない.

steps.title: Pattern & shortcuts
steps.body: Polite negative is preferred with strangers.
bullets: 食べます → 食べません
高いです → 高くないです
学生です → 学生ではありません / 学生じゃないです
In casual speech, ない and じゃない are common.

phrases.target: スペイン語を話しません。
コーヒーが好きじゃないです。
肉は決して食べません。
ここには何もありません。

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese negative form with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I don’t like coffee.":
steps.targetSentence: コーヒーが好きじゃないです。
steps.explanation: The negation pattern in its simplest form — learn it once, use it everywhere.

steps.title: Listen · negative
steps.prompt: Which is the polite negative of “食べます”?

steps.partnerSays: コーヒーが好き？
steps.prompt: Say no, you don't like it:
options: いいえ、好きじゃないです。
いいえ、好きくないです。
steps.correctAnswer: いいえ、好きじゃないです。
steps.explanation: 好き is a な-adjective, so its polite negative is 好きじゃないです (or 好きではありません). 〜くない is only for い-adjectives.

steps.title: Check · placement
steps.prompt: How do you make the polite negative of a ます verb?
options: Add ない after ます
Replace ます with ません
Add ありません before the verb
steps.explanation: ます → ません.

steps.title: Check · adjective
steps.prompt: How do you say “it’s not expensive”?
steps.explanation: い-adjective: drop い, add くないです.

title: Asking questions
description: Yes/no and information questions in Japanese.

steps.title: Question particle か
steps.body: Add か at the end of a statement to make a polite question. Rising intonation alone also works in casual speech.

steps.title: Three common patterns
steps.body: Same question, different levels of formality.
bullets: Rising intonation: コーヒーが好き？ (casual)
か: コーヒーが好きですか？ (polite)
Question word + か: どこですか？ / 何ですか？

phrases.target: どこに住んでいますか？
なぜ笑っているんですか？

steps.prompt: Match each Japanese question word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Do you speak English?":
steps.targetSentence: 英語を話しますか？
steps.explanation: A well-formed question using the key structure — polite, clear, and natural.

steps.title: Listen · why
steps.prompt: What does “なぜ” mean?

steps.partnerSays: 何か聞きたいことある？
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Is there something you want to ask?
steps.prompt: Politely ask where she lives:
options: どこに住んでいますか？
住んでいますかどこに？
steps.correctAnswer: どこに住んでいますか？
steps.explanation: Polite questions keep normal word order and end with か. Without か it's a statement, and か must come at the end.

steps.title: Check · polite question
steps.prompt: Which is the polite way to ask “Do you like coffee?”
options: コーヒーが好きですか？
steps.explanation: Statement + か (or ですか) is the polite question form.

steps.title: Check · word meaning
steps.prompt: “なぜ” means…
steps.explanation: なぜ / どうして = why.
